screens.title: ROS Actions in C++ and Asynchronous Operation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why production robotics often uses C++ for action servers, and how ROS actionlib maps high-level goals to multiple underlying topics. We'll show you a class-based SimpleActionServer pattern, how boost::bind connects class methods to callbacks, and the four client callbacks that let your node stay responsive while work is ongoing. You will see a concrete C++ server and client example for a CountUntil action, learn why add_dependencies is essential in CMake, and practice visualizing the five topics an action creates with rqt_graph. This matters because robots must handle motion, sensing, and manipulation with low latency and safe preemption. A quick example: a C++ navigation action can be preempted mid-path when an obstacle appears, delivering feedback during execution so higher-level controllers make decisions. Common misconceptions include thinking callbacks block the main thread — asynchronous callbacks keep the node responsive. By the end, you should feel confident writing a SimpleActionServer in C++, wiring a non-blocking client, and verifying topic-level behavior with rqt_graph. How will you use asynchronous callbacks to keep your robot multitasking safely?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will build in the lab. First, you will implement a SimpleActionServer in C++ using callback-based goal handling so your server can accept goals, publish feedback, and set results or preempt when needed. Second, you will implement a SimpleActionClient in C++ with asynchronous callbacks for feedback, activation, and final result, allowing the client to remain responsive while the action runs. Third, you will learn to handle goal preemption and cancellation inside the server, a safety-critical skill when higher-level controllers must interrupt long-running tasks. Fourth, you will use rqt_graph to visualize the action-related topics an action creates, which helps you debug connectivity and confirm language interoperability between Python and C++. Each objective includes a short explanation and a small visual mnemonic so you remember the skill: a server class box, client mailboxes, a preemption stop sign, and a network cluster for rqt_graph. These objectives let you write, compile, and run C++ action nodes and reason about their runtime behavior in integrated robot systems.

screens.title: Why use C++ for action servers?
screens.narratorSegment: C++ is commonly used for action servers in production because it gives you finer control over performance and memory, which matters for low-latency tasks like motor control or high-frequency sensor handling. In ROS, actions typically drive behavior that must be responsive to changes and capable of being interrupted. A C++ server written as a class with an internal SimpleActionServer member avoids copying large messages, uses ConstPtr semantics for goals, and lets you tightly manage loops and rates. For example, a navigation action counting steps must publish feedback at 2 hertz and check for preemption between iterations; C++ gives deterministic control over that loop. A common misconception is that Python cannot write safe action servers — Python is fine for prototyping, but in systems where latency or memory predictability matters, C++ is preferred. Another confusion arises around copying goals: using ConstPtr avoids unnecessary copying, saving C P U and memory. Takeaway: choose C++ when the action's real-time characteristics, frequent feedback, or resource constraints demand lower-level control. How will you decide when to switch a prototype action to C++ in your robot?

keyIdea.text: C++ action servers provide lower latency and finer resource control, making them suitable for production robotics where responsiveness and preemption safety are critical.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › Why C++?
Why prefer C++ for action servers
C++ gives low-level control over loops, memory, and blocking behavior needed for safe, responsive actions.
Claim
C++ reduces latency and avoids unnecessary copies by using ConstPtr goal types and explicit loop control.
Example
A CountUntil server publishes feedback at 2 Hz and checks isPreemptRequested each iteration to cancel promptly if requested.
Misconception
Python is not inherently unsafe for actions, but it may not meet strict timing or memory constraints of production hardware.
Analogy
Think of Python as a high-level workshop tool that speeds development. C++ is the precision lathe you bring when parts must fit tightly and tolerances are small. For time-critical robotic behavior, you reach for C++.
Practical check
  • Use ConstPtr to avoid copying goals.
  • Control loop rate explicitly with ros::Rate when publishing feedback.
  • Check isPreemptRequested frequently in loops and call setPreempted to stop safely.
Key Takeaway

Choose C++ when action latency, predictable memory, and safe preemption are required; use ConstPtr and explicit loop control to implement responsive servers.

screens.title: SimpleActionServer as a C++ class
screens.narratorSegment: A typical C++ SimpleActionServer is implemented as a class with a SimpleActionServer member named _as and an execute callback method. This design encapsulates server state and uses a constructor to create the server and bind the class method using boost::bind. The bind wraps the member function and the this pointer so the action server can call the method with a goal argument. The executeCB receives a ConstPtr to the goal type, which avoids copying large messages. Inside the callback you publish feedback messages, monitor isPreemptRequested, and setSucceeded or setPreempted accordingly. Concrete example: the CountUntilServer class constructs _as with nh, the action name, and boost::bind(&CountUntilServer::executeCB, this, _1). The _1 placeholder is the goal pointer the action server provides at runtime. A common mistake is attempting to pass a member function directly without binding, which fails because member functions need an object context. Takeaway: structure your server as a class so internal members, state, and ros handles are scoped and reusable; boost::bind connects the pieces so callbacks work reliably. SimpleActionServer as a C++ class means encapsulate simpleactionserver as a class member, use boost::bind to attach executecb, and accept goals as constptr to avoid copying.. In practical terms, member _as, constructor binding, and executecb signature. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Encapsulate SimpleActionServer as a class member, use boost::bind to attach executeCB, and accept goals as ConstPtr to avoid copying.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › Server Architecture
Class-based server pattern
Keep the server stateful inside a class so callbacks access member data and ROS handles cleanly.
Key fields
  • actionlib::SimpleActionServer<MyAction> _as;
  • executeCB(const MyActionGoalConstPtr& goal)
  • constructor binds method with boost::bind
Common mistake
Trying to pass a member function as a callback without boost::bind, which fails because the server needs a callable with an object bound to it.
Example snippet
#include <actionlib/server/simple_action_server.h>

class CountUntilServer {
public:
  CountUntilServer(ros::NodeHandle& nh) :
    _as(nh, "/count_until", boost::bind(&CountUntilServer::executeCB, this, _1), false) {
    _as.start();
  }

  void executeCB(const my_first_robot::CountUntilGoalConstPtr& goal) {
    // loop, publish feedback, handle preemption
  }

private:
  actionlib::SimpleActionServer<my_first_robot::CountUntilAction> _as;
};
Key Takeaway

Bind member methods with boost::bind so the action server can call the class's execute callback with a goal pointer and object context.

screens.title: Execute callback: feedback, preemption, and result
screens.narratorSegment: The execute callback is the heart of a SimpleActionServer: it receives the goal, performs work, publishes feedback, and finally sets the result or preempts. In the CountUntil example the callback reads the requested max_number, then loops from one to that value. At each iteration it publishes a feedback message with a percentage, calls rate. sleep to control the loop frequency, and checks _as. isPreemptRequested to see if a cancel or new goal arrived. If preemption is requested, the server calls _as. setPreempted and exits early. If the loop completes, the server constructs a result, calls _as. setSucceeded, and returns. A common confusion is thinking setPreempted takes a boolean or is optional; you must explicitly call setPreempted to inform the action client the goal did not complete. Example scenario: a navigation goal is canceled when an obstacle appears; the server must stop motor commands and call setPreempted so higher-level logic can react. Misconception: publishFeedback is expensive—it's lightweight but choose a sensible rate, like 2 Hz in the example. Closing takeaway: keep the loop responsive and call the correct terminal A P I to communicate final state.

keyIdea.title: Execution flow
keyIdea.text: Inside executeCB, loop with a controlled rate, publish feedback, check isPreemptRequested to handle cancels, and call setSucceeded or setPreempted as appropriate.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › Execute callback
Feedback and preemption pattern
Publish periodic feedback, check preemption, and set the appropriate terminal state so clients know the outcome.
Loop structure
  • Create ros::Rate for feedback frequency (e.g., 2 Hz).
  • On each iteration publish feedback.percentage and sleep.
  • If isPreemptRequested return early and call setPreempted.
Misconception
Feedback floods are costly: choose a sensible frequency. publishFeedback is inexpensive but sending many messages can overload downstream handlers.
Example snippet
void executeCB(const my_first_robot::CountUntilGoalConstPtr& goal) {
  bool success = true;
  ros::Rate rate(2); // 2 Hz feedback

  for (int i = 1; i <= goal->max_number; ++i) {
    if (_as.isPreemptRequested()) {
      _as.setPreempted();
      success = false;
      break;
    }

    my_first_robot::CountUntilFeedback feedback;
    feedback.percentage = float(i) / float(goal->max_number);
    _as.publishFeedback(feedback);
    rate.sleep();
  }

  if (success) {
    my_first_robot::CountUntilResult result;
    result.count = goal->max_number;
    _as.setSucceeded(result);
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Keep callbacks responsive: check preemption in each loop iteration and explicitly set a terminal state so clients can react correctly.

screens.title: CMakeLists and add_dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: When building C++ nodes that use custom action messages, a common compilation failure comes from missing generated headers. Action headers are created during message generation in the catkin build process, so your CMakeLists must declare a dependency on the message target. The add_dependencies line tells catkin that the executable depends on the exported targets from the package that generates the action headers. Without that dependency the compiler may run before the headers exist, producing a missing header error. The provided CMake snippet finds required packages, creates an executable, and adds add_dependencies(count_until_server ${my_first_robot_EXPORTED_TARGETS}) before linking libraries. Practical example: if your package my_first_robot defines CountUntil. action, adding the exported targets ensures CountUntilAction. h is available when count_until_server. cpp compiles. Misconception: add_dependencies is not optional for generated code; it prevents race conditions during parallel builds. Takeaway: always add dependencies on message/action-generated targets when compiling C++ nodes that include generated headers. CMakeLists and add_dependencies means use add_dependencies in cmakelists to force generation of action message headers before compiling c++ sources that include them.. In practical terms, ensure action headers are generated before compiling your c++ node. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › CMakeLists
CMake and generated headers
Prevent compile-time races by declaring dependencies on generated action/message targets.
Why it matters
Catkin may build message generation and C++ compilation in parallel. add_dependencies forces the right order so CountUntilAction.h exists when compiling.
Snippet
find_package(catkin REQUIRED COMPONENTS
  roscpp
  actionlib
  actionlib_msgs
  my_first_robot
)

add_executable(count_until_server src/count_until_server.cpp)
add_dependencies(count_until_server ${my_first_robot_EXPORTED_TARGETS})
target_link_libraries(count_until_server ${catkin_LIBRARIES})
Common mistake
Omitting add_dependencies leads to missing header errors during parallel builds. Adding the dependency is the correct solution, not moving code around.
Key Takeaway

Declare add_dependencies for executables that include generated action headers so the build system generates messages before compilation.

screens.title: SimpleActionClient in C++ and callbacks
screens.narratorSegment: A robust C++ SimpleActionClient uses four important interactions: waitForServer to ensure the server is available, sendGoal with bound callbacks, and optional cancelGoal for preemption from the client side. The client class often holds a SimpleActionClient member, waits for the server at startup, then sends goals using boost::bind to connect done, active, and feedback callbacks. doneCB receives the final SimpleClientGoalState and a result pointer so you can log completion state and data. activeCB informs you the goal became active on the server, and feedbackCB receives periodic progress updates. For example, a CountUntilClient waits for the server, sends a goal of max_number 10, receives feedback percentage updates, and after a delay may call cancelGoal to request cancellation. A misconception is assuming waitForServer blocks forever; it blocks until the server advertises or until you implement a timeout. Design clients to handle server unavailability gracefully. Takeaway: structured callbacks let clients remain responsive and monitor multiple simultaneous goals without blocking the main thread. SimpleActionClient in C++ and callbacks means bind done, active, and feedback callbacks so the client stays asynchronous; use waitforserver and cancelgoal to coordinate interactions safely.. In practical terms, donecb, activecb, feedbackcb and waitforserver/sendgoal patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Client callbacks
keyIdea.text: Bind done, active, and feedback callbacks so the client stays asynchronous; use waitForServer and cancelGoal to coordinate interactions safely.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › Client Architecture
Async client callbacks explained
Use callbacks for done, active, and feedback so your node remains responsive and can manage multiple actions.
Callback roles
  • activeCB: goal accepted and now executing.
  • feedbackCB: periodic progress updates.
  • doneCB: final state and result available.
Design tip
Use non-blocking patterns and avoid heavy work in callbacks; instead, post updates to the main loop or use thread-safe containers.
Example snippet
_ac.sendGoal(goal,
             boost::bind(&CountUntilClient::doneCB, this, _1, _2),
             boost::bind(&CountUntilClient::activeCB, this),
             boost::bind(&CountUntilClient::feedbackCB, this, _1));

// callbacks
void feedbackCB(const my_first_robot::CountUntilFeedbackConstPtr& feedback) { /* ... */ }
void activeCB() { /* ... */ }
void doneCB(const actionlib::SimpleClientGoalState& state,
            const my_first_robot::CountUntilResultConstPtr& result) { /* ... */ }
Key Takeaway

Bind your callbacks and avoid blocking the main thread so a client can handle multiple simultaneous actions and feedback streams.

screens.title: Asynchronous operation and multi-action monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Asynchronous operation means the client does not block while waiting for the server to finish a goal. Instead, it registers callbacks and continues other work. This is essential for robots that must monitor sensors or run other actions simultaneously. A practical approach is to create a client object for each server you want to monitor, send separate goals with bound callbacks for each, and keep a lightweight main loop that handles coordination, logging, or cancellation decisions. For example, a combined C++ client can send a goal to /count_until and another to /count_until_fast; each client instance receives feedbackCB calls independently and reports progress. If one action must be canceled based on sensor input, call cancelGoal on that client; the server will detect preemption and call setPreempted. A common pitfall is running long blocking computations inside callbacks, which starves the client of responsiveness. Instead, keep callbacks small and hand off heavy processing to worker threads or the main loop. Takeaway: design clients and callbacks so the program can monitor multiple actions, handle cancellations, and remain responsive to new goals or sensor events.

narration.text: Asynchronous operation means the client does not block while waiting for the server to finish a goal. Instead, it registers callbacks and continues other work. This is essential for robots that must monitor sensors or run other actions simultaneously. A practical approach is to create a client object for each server you want to monitor, send separate goals with bound callbacks for each, and keep a lightweight main loop that handles coordination, logging, or cancellation decisions. A common pitfall is running long blocking computations inside callbacks, which starves the client of responsiveness. Instead, keep callbacks small and hand off heavy processing to worker threads or the main loop. screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging patterns
screens.narratorSegment: This slide lists common errors encountered when implementing C++ action servers and how to debug them reliably. First, missing generated headers during compilation usually indicate add_dependencies was not declared in CMakeLists; fix this by adding the exported targets for your message package. Second, name mismatches between client and server prevent topic connections; rqt_graph will show missing links when the names differ. Third, forgetting to call setPreempted leaves the client waiting — always call the terminal A P I to communicate state. Fourth, placing heavy computations inside callbacks blocks the node and prevents processing other callbacks or ROS timers. When you see no feedback arriving, check that publishFeedback is called at a sensible rate and that the client subscribed to the correct feedback topic. For runtime debugging, use ROS_INFO logging in callbacks to trace execution and run rqt_graph to inspect topic wiring. Takeaway: systematic checks—build dependencies, exact names, correct terminal calls, and minimal callback work—resolve most common issues. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why production robotics often uses C++ for action servers, and how ROS actionlib maps high-level goals to multiple underlying topics. We'll show you a class-based SimpleActionServer pattern, how boost::bind connects class methods to callbacks, and the four client callbacks that let your node stay responsive while work is ongoing. You will see a concrete C++ server and client example for a CountUntil action, learn why add_dependencies is essential in CMake, and practice visualizing the five topics an action creates with rqt_graph. This matters because robots must handle motion, sensing, and manipulation with low latency and safe preemption. A quick example: a C++ navigation action can be preempted mid-path when an obstacle appears, delivering feedback during execution so higher-level controllers make decisions. Common misconceptions include thinking callbacks block the main thread — asynchronous callbacks keep the node responsive. By the end, you should feel confident writing a SimpleActionServer in C++, wiring a non-blocking client, and verifying topic-level behavior with rqt_graph. How will you use asynchronous callbacks to keep your robot multitasking safely?

These objectives map to practical skills you will build in the lab. First, you will implement a SimpleActionServer in C++ using callback-based goal handling so your server can accept goals, publish feedback, and set results or preempt when needed. Second, you will implement a SimpleActionClient in C++ with asynchronous callbacks for feedback, activation, and final result, allowing the client to remain responsive while the action runs. Third, you will learn to handle goal preemption and cancellation inside the server, a safety-critical skill when higher-level controllers must interrupt long-running tasks. Fourth, you will use rqt_graph to visualize the action-related topics an action creates, which helps you debug connectivity and confirm language interoperability between Python and C++. Each objective includes a short explanation and a small visual mnemonic so you remember the skill: a server class box, client mailboxes, a preemption stop sign, and a network cluster for rqt_graph. These objectives let you write, compile, and run C++ action nodes and reason about their runtime behavior in integrated robot systems.

This page explains the practical outcomes you will confirm in the lab. You will compile a C++ action server and verify it accepts goals from a Python client, proving the ROS action protocol is language-agnostic. Next, swap roles and run the Python server with your C++ client to confirm cross-language result and feedback delivery. You will run rqt_graph with Actions checked and then unchecked to see how actionlib groups topics into a single action block and, when expanded, reveals five underlying topics. In a follow-up task, you will write a combined C++ client that sends two simultaneous goals to different servers and monitor both feedback streams with separate callbacks. Verify that the main thread remains responsive and that cancelGoal cleanly requests cancellation. These verifications ensure you can both build and debug action-based systems and understand common build mistakes that prevent headers from being found at compile time.

C++ is commonly used for action servers in production because it gives you finer control over performance and memory, which matters for low-latency tasks like motor control or high-frequency sensor handling. In ROS, actions typically drive behavior that must be responsive to changes and capable of being interrupted. A C++ server written as a class with an internal SimpleActionServer member avoids copying large messages, uses ConstPtr semantics for goals, and lets you tightly manage loops and rates. For example, a navigation action counting steps must publish feedback at 2 hertz and check for preemption between iterations; C++ gives deterministic control over that loop. A common misconception is that Python cannot write safe action servers — Python is fine for prototyping, but in systems where latency or memory predictability matters, C++ is preferred. Another confusion arises around copying goals: using ConstPtr avoids unnecessary copying, saving C P U and memory. Takeaway: choose C++ when the action's real-time characteristics, frequent feedback, or resource constraints demand lower-level control. How will you decide when to switch a prototype action to C++ in your robot?

A typical C++ SimpleActionServer is implemented as a class with a SimpleActionServer member named _as and an execute callback method. This design encapsulates server state and uses a constructor to create the server and bind the class method using boost::bind. The bind wraps the member function and the this pointer so the action server can call the method with a goal argument. The executeCB receives a ConstPtr to the goal type, which avoids copying large messages. Inside the callback you publish feedback messages, monitor isPreemptRequested, and setSucceeded or setPreempted accordingly. Concrete example: the CountUntilServer class constructs _as with nh, the action name, and boost::bind(&CountUntilServer::executeCB, this, _1). The _1 placeholder is the goal pointer the action server provides at runtime. A common mistake is attempting to pass a member function directly without binding, which fails because member functions need an object context. Takeaway: structure your server as a class so internal members, state, and ros handles are scoped and reusable; boost::bind connects the pieces so callbacks work reliably. SimpleActionServer as a C++ class means encapsulate simpleactionserver as a class member, use boost::bind to attach executecb, and accept goals as constptr to avoid copying.. In practical terms, member _as, constructor binding, and executecb signature. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The execute callback is the heart of a SimpleActionServer: it receives the goal, performs work, publishes feedback, and finally sets the result or preempts. In the CountUntil example the callback reads the requested max_number, then loops from one to that value. At each iteration it publishes a feedback message with a percentage, calls rate. sleep to control the loop frequency, and checks _as. isPreemptRequested to see if a cancel or new goal arrived. If preemption is requested, the server calls _as. setPreempted and exits early. If the loop completes, the server constructs a result, calls _as. setSucceeded, and returns. A common confusion is thinking setPreempted takes a boolean or is optional; you must explicitly call setPreempted to inform the action client the goal did not complete. Example scenario: a navigation goal is canceled when an obstacle appears; the server must stop motor commands and call setPreempted so higher-level logic can react. Misconception: publishFeedback is expensive—it's lightweight but choose a sensible rate, like 2 Hz in the example. Closing takeaway: keep the loop responsive and call the correct terminal A P I to communicate final state.

When building C++ nodes that use custom action messages, a common compilation failure comes from missing generated headers. Action headers are created during message generation in the catkin build process, so your CMakeLists must declare a dependency on the message target. The add_dependencies line tells catkin that the executable depends on the exported targets from the package that generates the action headers. Without that dependency the compiler may run before the headers exist, producing a missing header error. The provided CMake snippet finds required packages, creates an executable, and adds add_dependencies(count_until_server ${my_first_robot_EXPORTED_TARGETS}) before linking libraries. Practical example: if your package my_first_robot defines CountUntil. action, adding the exported targets ensures CountUntilAction. h is available when count_until_server. cpp compiles.
